name: Three-phase circuit with neutral and PE marking
aliases: L1 L2 L3 N PE notation
summary: A single-line notation such as 3/N/PE showing a three-phase circuit carrying both a neutral and a separate protective conductor.
description: Single-line diagrams often state the conductor complement of a circuit with a short notation beside the line, for example 3/N/PE 400/230 V 50 Hz. This tells the reader at a glance that the circuit has three phases, a neutral and a separate protective conductor, which is the normal TN-S final distribution arrangement.

The notation is a statement about which conductors exist, not their sizes. It also does not confirm that the downstream equipment uses the neutral. Changes in the notation along a feeder, for example from 3/PEN to 3/N/PE, mark the point where a PEN conductor has been split.
readingNotes: Watch for a change in notation along a feeder that marks a PEN split.
Read voltage and frequency that may follow the conductor notation.
drawingChecklist: State the conductor complement on each distribution feeder.
Include voltage and frequency where the notation is used.
Keep notation consistent with the cable schedule.
distinction: The 3/N/PE notation states a whole conductor complement; individual N, PE or PEN marks identify one conductor on a stroke.
